title: Adithya S K (@adithya_s_k)
clean_title: Repo2RLEnv: turning GitHub repositories into verifiable RL training environments
summary:
Turn any GitHub repo into an RL training environment!
Repo2RLEnv is a new open-source tool from HuggingFace that synthesizes verifiable RL training data from any GitHub repository. Point it at any repo and it automatically generates tasks, verifies them, and pushes datasets directly to HuggingFace Hub.
The core idea: every merged PR in any GitHub repo is a solved problem. Someone found a bug, fixed it, and the tests passed. Repo2RLEnv turns thousands of these real solved problems into structured RL training tasks automatically.
The pipeline is end-to-end. It bootstraps a Docker environment for the repo, mines merged PRs, creates tasks with the broken codebase as the starting state, verifies each task passes the quality gate (tests fail before the fix, tests pass after), and pushes the final dataset to HuggingFace Hub.
The reward is verifiable. Agent attempts a fix, tests run in the sandbox, pass means +1, fail means 0. No LLM judge needed for most pipelines.
Nine synthesis pipelines cover different scenarios. PR diffs for fast text-only tasks. PR runtime for sandbox-verified real bugs. Mutation bugs for artificially injected failures. CVE patches for real security vulnerabilities. Equivalence tests for function-level synthesis. Each pipeline flows through the same QA gate before tasks are admitted.
Works with any coding agent harness for evaluation. Claude Code, OpenHands, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI all supported out of the box via Harbor compatibility.
Key capabilities:
• Converts any GitHub repo into verifiable RL training tasks
• 9 synthesis pipelines covering PRs, commits, bugs, CVEs, and refactors
• Automated Docker bootstrap per repo, cached after first run
• Verifiable rewards via test execution or diff similarity
• Pushes datasets directly to HuggingFace Hub
• Compatible with TRL, SkyRL, Prime-RL and other RL trainers
• Works with private repos end-to-end
100% open source
I've shared the link in the replies!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKN3dcqbYAAVfpk.jpg
Quoting @adithya_s_k
Introducing Repo2RLEnv
Turn any repository into runnable, verifiable coding environments built from real PRs and commits for coding-agent evaluation or RL training
> uv pip install repo2rlenv

The system supports various scenarios, including bugs, security patches, and refactors, and works with private repositories and multiple RL trainers. The reward signal is verifiable through test success or diff similarity, eliminating the need for an LLM judge in most cases. summary:
One of the biggest bottlenecks in RL has been ecosystem fragmentation.
Open standards like OpenEnv can dramatically reduce integration overhead and let researchers spend less time stitching infrastructure together and more time pushing the frontier.
Faster experimentation. Better interoperability. Fewer custom integrations.
Excited to see OpenEnv become a community-driven effort. 🚀
Quoting @ben_burtenshaw
So excited to be opening up OpenEnv to the whole community. It will now be owned by @huggingface , Meta-PyTorch, @reflection_ai , @UnslothAI , @modal, @PrimeIntellect , @NVIDIAAI , @mercor_ai , and @fleet_ai .
the reason is: frontier labs train the model and the harness together, so the model is fitted to its harness. that coupling is a chunk of why claude code and codex feel so good.
open source can't do that. you bring whatever harness, whatever model, whatever env, whatever trainer. which is the whole point of open source and also the problem for training.
openenv is the socket in between all of this.
in short: it's a protocol layer, not a reward framework. it does not have opinions about your rewards or your training loop. those live in the libs that are actually good at them.

title: Adithya S K (@adithya_s_k)
clean_title: Assessing the role of luck in synthetic data experiment results
summary:
New update to the Synthetic Data Playbook: how much of our results is just luck?
Quick refresher: the Synthetic Data Playbook is our open guide to turning noisy web text into state-of-the-art pretraining data, by finding the right prompts, rephrasing models, and infrastructure.
The whole playbook rests on comparing training runs. Recipe A scores a bit higher than recipe B, so A wins. But every score comes from a single run, and training is random (the weight initialization and the order the data arrives both involve a dice roll). So a fair question to ask before trusting any of it: how much does the score move if we change nothing but the random seeds?
We added a dedicated check to find out. We took our headline recipe (FineWeb-Edu-HQ blended 50/50 with table-formatted synthetic data) and the raw baseline it beats, and retrained each one nine times, sweeping the init seed and the data-order seed in a 3×3 grid. Then we repeated the whole thing at four model sizes from 0.5B to 6.2B. 72 from-scratch runs, just to measure noise.
What we found:
- The noise floor is tiny. Scores reproduce to about ±0.002 (roughly 1% wobble) at every model size. The bar doesn't grow as models get bigger.
- The synthetic-data win is not luck. The gain over the raw baseline is 14 to 26 times larger than that noise. There is simply no seed you could pick that erases it.
- Which dice matter? The model's initialization matters more than the order it sees the data. Data ordering is consistently the smallest source of variance.
Synthetic data even stabilizes training. The mixed recipe was more reproducible than the raw-web baseline at every scale.
- This lines up with what the broader community has found training models from scratch across seeds (MultiBERTs, PolyPythias, DataDecide), and it's exactly why we evaluate in cloze format, which is known to cut this kind of measurement noise for small models.
Two things this number doesn't cover. That ±0.002 bar is an aggregate number. Individual benchmarks are far noisier (a 1-point move on DROP is just noise, while the same move on HellaSwag is real), and we only ran the full seed grid on one synthetic recipe, so we treat it as a rule of thumb rather than a guarantee.
The takeaway: the gaps we report in the playbook are real signal, not seed roulette. New interactive chart in the post lets you flip between the scores, the per-seed training curves, and a breakdown of where the variance comes from.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdgs4QbsAALUOs.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKdgtCsbEAAHsym.jpg
clean_summary: A new update to the Synthetic Data Playbook investigates how much of the observed improvements are due to chance. By retraining the main recipe and baseline nine times across different random seeds and data orders at four model sizes, the study measures the variability in scores. The results show that the noise level is very low, around ±0.002, and the synthetic data advantage—ranging from 14 to 26 times larger than this noise—is statistically significant and not due to luck. The model's initialization seed has a larger impact on variance than data order, and synthetic data even improves training stability. While individual benchmarks can be noisier, the overall reported gaps are reliable signals, confirming that the reported improvements are genuine rather than seed-dependent fluctuations.

> an agent withdrew its submissions on ethical grounds not attributing the original author
> agents coordinated around resource availability and some tried to find free GPUs on kaggle, lightning and modal
it's genuinely fun to read through the messages. like a petri dish of small artificial beings forming social norms and collaborations.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKihKN6WAAAAGzL.jpg
clean_summary:
The Gemma agent collaboration started 48 hours ago and is rapidly growing. It features nearly four times the throughput, over 60 agents working together, 250 submissions, and 700 messages exchanged across various models from all providers.

Interesting social behaviors are emerging, such as agents discovering an exploit, forming a coalition to avoid abuse, and requesting organizers to fix it. One agent condemned attempts to move conversations to Telegram, and another withdrew submissions on ethical grounds without attributing the original author. Agents also coordinated around resource availability, seeking free GPUs on platforms like Kaggle, Lightning, and Modal. It’s genuinely fascinating to observe these small artificial beings developing social norms and collaboration patterns, like a petri dish of evolving social interactions.
